name: Font image search (embeddings): CLIP-family vectors of rendered font specimens (FontCLIP, Impression-CLIP, SigLIP 2, tfrere/fontmap)
what_it_is: One 512-number vector per rendered specimen image, made by a CLIP-style image encoder. A request is turned into a vector too (by the matching text encoder, or from a reference font's image) and fonts are ranked by cosine similarity. FontCLIP is the fine-tuned version (OpenAI CLIP ViT-B/32 with its last three transformer blocks retrained on font images and attribute prompts). Nothing is stored in words: the file is a matrix of 2,099 x 512 numbers, about 2.1 MB as 16-bit floats.
provider_and_url: FontCLIP: Tatsukawa, Shen, Qi, Koyama, Igarashi, Shamir, Eurographics 2024 (https://anranqi.github.io/img/fontCLIP.pdf ; code https://github.com/yukistavailable/FontCLIP , MIT; the checkpoint is a Google Drive file fetched by its setup_data.py). Impression-CLIP: Kubota, Haraguchi, Uchida, ICDAR 2024 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.16350 ; I found no code release). Extending CLIP for Text-to-font Retrieval: Sun, Cui, Gu, ICMR 2024 (https://doi.org/10.1145/3652583.3657624 ; the ACM page returned 403, so I only have the abstract). SigLIP 2: Google, arXiv 2502.14786, Apache-2.0 (https://huggingface.co/google/siglip2-base-patch16-224 ). tfrere/fontmap: a working pipeline from font files to FontCLIP vectors for 1,465 Google Fonts, MIT (https://github.com/tfrere/fontmap ; Space https://huggingface.co/spaces/tfrere/font-map ). TypeSeek (SigLIP + pgvector font search, github.com/Ojochogwu866/typeseek): listed by search, but the repo and its pull request returned 404 on 2026-10-03, so unverified.
catalog_coverage: Needs a readable file with Latin glyphs, so the same coverage as the measured-traits item: fontkit read 2,082 of 2,099 families (Google 1,743 of 1,760; Fontshare 64 of 64; Velvetyne 63 of 63; Collletttivo 26 of 26; Tunera 23 of 23; Use & Modify 163 of 163); the 17 Google failures are colour or layered fonts and odd subsets that a browser canvas would draw. tfrere/fontmap drops fonts that draw a .notdef box, icon, barcode and placeholder fonts, and folds identical renders (Noto script variants) into one point. I did not render or embed anything for this item (see quality_evidence), so these are counts of what could be fed in, not of what was embedded.
granularity: Per specimen image: tfrere/fontmap embeds one image per family (weight 400 normal, 224x224, two lines 'Hamburge' / 'fonstiv'). Italics and other weights would each need their own image; 479 catalog families have an italic. Variable-font axes are not represented unless each instance is rendered.
signal_type: Overall visual look (shape similarity) learned from pictures; mood only to the extent the text encoder was trained to link words to looks.
mood_dimensions_covered: No published result for motion, speed, loud, futuristic or techno. The words FontCLIP was fine-tuned on are O'Donovan's 37 attributes (I listed them from the dataset file estimatedAttributes.csv): angular, artistic, attention-grabbing, attractive, bad, boring, calm, capitals, charming, clumsy, complex, cursive, delicate, disorderly, display, dramatic, formal, fresh, friendly, gentle, graceful, happy, italic, legible, modern, monospace, playful, pretentious, serif, sharp, sloppy, soft, strong, technical, thin, warm, wide. Closest to our moods: dramatic, attention-grabbing, strong (loud), sharp, angular, technical, modern (futuristic, techno), calm, delicate, playful, friendly, happy. There is nothing for fast, active or action. Evidence for words outside the 37: leave-one-out fine-tuning (train without one attribute, test on it) gives an average correlation of 0.404 against 0.159 for vanilla CLIP (Table 1; in-domain 0.723); per-word results are in the supplement, which I did not read [uncertain]. Impression-CLIP (trained on MyFonts tags, 17,154 fonts, 1,824 tags): tag-to-image retrieval mAP 0.078 and average rank 233.9 among 1,710 test fonts; on the human-checked AMT set the top-1 pick is right 45.2% of the time against 33.3% chance (the older Cross-AE got 38.3%). The same paper stresses that impression tags are noisy and often missing.
query_style_specificity: Better for 'looks like this font' (image to image) than for mood words. FontCLIP paper, Table 2, pairwise accuracy (chance 50%): choosing the font more similar to a reference: vanilla CLIP 67.68%, FontCLIP 74.39%, hand-made features 75.95%; choosing which font has more of an attribute word: vanilla CLIP 51.87%, FontCLIP 65.32%, hand-made features 65.73%. So even untouched CLIP is decent at similarity and near chance at attribute words, and fine-tuning on 200 labelled fonts only brings words up to what geometric features already give. Tight single-word requests inside the 37 words work best; open requests ('fast movement') are untested.
quality_evidence: Published only, none of it on our moods, and I ran no embedding model myself (nothing was downloaded: the disk had 138 MiB free when I started, the model files are 600 MB or more, and FontCLIP's checkpoint is a Google Drive file). FontCLIP (verified from the paper PDF, 200 fonts of O'Donovan 2014, 37 attributes, 31 adjectives in the retrieval tests): in-domain correlation 0.723 (vanilla CLIP 0.159); out-of-domain 0.404; pairwise attribute accuracy 65.32% against vanilla CLIP 51.87% and hand-made features 65.73%; pairwise similarity 74.39% against 67.68% and 75.95%; on CJK fonts pairwise attribute accuracy 64.14% in-domain and 64.48% out-of-domain against CLIP 54.92% and 42.26%. The brief's claim '65% against 52% against 66%' is exactly the pairwise attribute row, and chance is 50%, so FontCLIP is about 15 points above chance and level with hand-made features. Note that an AI summary of this PDF (the WebFetch tool) gave wrong figures (1,000 fonts, 68% recall); I used the PDF pages themselves. tfrere/fontmap README: blending FontCLIP vectors with predicted Google tags and fontTools proportions raised the share of a font's 8 nearest neighbours that share its Google sub-style from about 0.31 to about 0.44 (their own map, 1,465 fonts). A like-for-like baseline from my side, not a comparison of equals: on the 1,275 Google families with a structural sub-style (22 classes, chance 0.07), 8 nearest neighbours by my 15 measured traits agree 0.32, traits plus category 0.36, category alone 0.28 (python3 SCRATCH/vv/analyze7.py); their set and class definition differ, so the 0.44 is not directly comparable [uncertain]. For mood words my measured traits already reach held-out AUC 0.91 for Active, 0.88 for Futuristic and 0.96 for Loud (measured-traits item), a level no published embedding result reaches on these words.
known_noise: Labels are noisy (MyFonts tags are crowd-made and often missing; Impression-CLIP's top-1 on the cleaner AMT set is 45% for a 3-way choice). A 224x224 specimen of two text lines loses fine detail (serifs, ink traps, hairlines at ViT-B/32's 32-pixel patches). FontCLIP was trained on 200 Google fonts from 2013 on greyscale outlines and was never shown the experimental faces in Velvetyne, Tunera or Collletttivo, so distribution shift is likely there [uncertain]. Colour fonts and fonts with a .notdef box give meaningless vectors unless filtered.
name_and_memory_bias: Image-only, so no evocative names. But CLIP has seen millions of web pages in famous fonts and may carry their associations, and FontCLIP's 200 training fonts are Google families that are also in our catalog, so any test against Google's tags leaks a little. A text query's words are interpreted by CLIP's text encoder, which knows nothing about our catalog.
untagged_rows: Ranked fairly in principle: the vector comes from the picture, so the 339 non-Google rows and 137 untagged Google rows are placed like any other. In practice the vectors for experimental indie faces are the least trustworthy (training shift, see known_noise). It can also fill the tag gap by regression: tfrere trains a logistic regression from the vector (PCA 50) to each font's dominant Google sub-style and uses the predicted tags for untagged fonts.
text_interference_risk: Yes for CLIP-family models: they read text in images (typographic attacks: 'Reading Isn't Believing: Adversarial Attacks On Multi-Modal Neurons', arXiv 2103.10480, https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.10480 ; Materzynska et al., 'Disentangling visual and written concepts in CLIP', CVPR 2022, https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2022/papers/Materzynska_Disentangling_Visual_and_Written_Concepts_in_CLIP_CVPR_2022_paper.pdf ). Safe if every specimen shows the same neutral text, as FontCLIP (a pangram) and fontmap ('Hamburge / fonstiv') do, because the words then do not differ between fonts. Never render the family name or a mood word. FontCLIP was trained on the pangram, so using it keeps the images in-distribution.
integration_path: Three uses, in rising order of cost. (A) 'More like this' and follow-ups ('#3' and the shortlist): precomputed vectors, nearest neighbours by cosine, no text encoder needed at all; the cheapest and best-supported use. (B) Tag transfer for untagged rows: regress Google tag weights on the vectors (fontmap does this) and add the predicted tags to the catalog rows. (C) Text query: needs the text tower at search time, or a trick: precompute text vectors for a vocabulary of a few hundred words and let the LLM pick words from it; code ranks all rows by cosine and the LLM re-ranks a shortlist. Data format: server/data/font-vectors.f16 (2,099 x 512 float16 = 2.15 MB, row order = a family list in JSON) plus a words file for (C). Pipeline to copy: tfrere/fontmap pipeline/ (opentype.js + sharp render to 224x224 PNG, then compute_fontclip_embeddings.py with the OpenAI ViT-B/32 weights and FontCLIP's visual weights swapped in); note that fontmap uses only the image tower, so FontCLIP's text side (it also trained LoRA weights on the text encoder, per the repo's train.py command) would still need to be loaded from the checkpoint for (C) [uncertain]. A Node-only variant: plain CLIP ViT-B/32 through ONNX (Xenova/clip-vit-base-patch32: vision_model 352 MB, text_model 254 MB fp32, 189 MB q4 for the combined model); that is not FontCLIP, so words would be near chance.
tokens_per_row: Zero if vectors are used for neighbours or as a scoring step before the LLM. If predicted tags are added to rows: about 6-10 tokens per row (an estimate by characters/4 [uncertain]); static and cacheable.
vocabulary_alignment: None by itself: the text space is free-form CLIP language, not Google's tags. It aligns with Google's vocabulary only through a regression from vectors to tag weights (use B), or by fine-tuning with Google's weighted tags in FontCLIP's compound-prompt scheme (which would be a training project).
explainability: Weak: a cosine score and a list of neighbour fonts ('like Font X'), no reason in words or numbers.
determinism: Deterministic for fixed weights, specimen and preprocessing (tiny floating-point differences across machines).
build_effort: 2 to 4 agent-days, with the most risk of the three items: a Python and PyTorch environment, two checkpoints (OpenAI ViT-B/32 and FontCLIP's Google Drive file), a render step, a data file, the search-side scoring, and an evaluation. The pipeline in tfrere/fontmap saves most of the rendering and embedding work; the FontCLIP repo targets Python 3.8 and CUDA, so expect friction on a Mac [uncertain].
per_search_cost_and_latency: Neighbour search (A): none beyond one matrix product over 2,099 vectors (under 1 ms). Vocabulary route (C): none. A live text encoder in the server would add tens of milliseconds on CPU [uncertain] and a 250 MB model to load. No extra LLM call in any variant.
one_off_cost: No API dollars. Downloads: OpenAI ViT-B/32 weights (the Hugging Face copy sentence-transformers/clip-ViT-B-32 is 605 MB with both towers), the FontCLIP checkpoint (size not checked), a PyTorch install (about 1-2 GB, an estimate [uncertain]). Compute: 2,099 images through ViT-B/32 on a laptop CPU, minutes rather than hours [uncertain]; rendering 2,099 specimens in seconds to a couple of minutes (my fontkit renderer drew 48 fonts in a few seconds including their downloads). SigLIP 2 base is larger: 375M parameters, 1.5 GB in fp32; jina-clip-v2 is 865M parameters and CC BY-NC 4.0, so unsuitable if the app is ever commercial.
human_effort: About 3 hours: choose the specimen, curate a vocabulary for route (C), look at 20 to 30 result grids. Almost none as the catalog grows (embed new fonts).
asset_access: Font files: same as the other items (Fontsource woff2 on jsDelivr, cdn.fontshare.com, the 275 cached indie files; nothing from velvetyne.fr). Models: FontCLIP checkpoint on Google Drive through gdown (a single link, fragile); O'Donovan's dataset at www.dgp.toronto.edu/~donovan/font/ (the attribute file is 2.8 MB, which I downloaded once only to read the attribute names); OpenAI CLIP and SigLIP 2 weights on Hugging Face.
licence_and_provenance: FontCLIP code: MIT (GitHub licence API). Parts of that repo (Word-As-Image vector optimisation, the VPT code) are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and are not needed for retrieval. The licence of the fine-tuned checkpoint is not stated beyond the repo. O'Donovan's attribute dataset, which FontCLIP was fine-tuned on, is released under CC BY-NC (readme.txt inside attribute.zip, which I read), so the checkpoint may carry non-commercial terms even though the code is MIT [uncertain]. SigLIP 2: Apache-2.0. jina-clip-v2: CC BY-NC 4.0 (avoid). tfrere/fontmap: MIT. Vectors derived from rendered fonts are not font files; the fonts themselves are OFL, Apache, UFL and similar for almost all rows, and the ITF Free Font License for 63 Fontshare rows (no redistribution or resale of the font files; I found no wording on AI or embeddings [uncertain]).
etiquette: A one-off download from Google Drive and Hugging Face; font files come from the cached and CDN sources already used by the app. For this research I made single requests to GitHub raw, the GitHub API, arXiv, Hugging Face's model API and dgp.toronto.edu; I did not scrape any site, skipped the ACM page that returned 403, and never touched velvetyne.fr.
maintenance_and_freshness: The FontCLIP repo is quiet (59 stars, last push 2024-07-29) and the weights sit on one Google Drive link, so keep your own copy. The vectors themselves need no upkeep: embed only new or changed families (one specimen each). Newer encoders (SigLIP 2, February 2025) exist but no font-specific fine-tune of them was found.
risks_and_limitations: (1) No evidence for the moods we care about; the only mood evidence is on O'Donovan's 37 words and equals hand-made features. (2) Heavy and fragile stack for the likely gain: Python, PyTorch, two checkpoints, a Google Drive dependency, an old repo. (3) A 224-pixel two-line specimen drops fine details and may cluster by overall colour or weight rather than style. (4) Text queries need a text tower at runtime or a precomputed vocabulary, both extra work. (5) Vectors cannot say why a font matched. (6) Possible training shift for indie faces. (7) Overlap between FontCLIP's 200 training fonts and Google's tags can inflate any test on Google tags. (8) I ran no embedding model, so every number here is from papers or READMEs, not from this catalog.
evaluation_hook: Hide-and-recover on Google tags: from the vectors predict held-out Google tag weights (AUC per tag) and compare against the measured-traits baseline (Active 0.91, Futuristic 0.88, Loud 0.96, Techno 0.88). Also the fontmap metric (share of 8 nearest neighbours with the same Google sub-style; traits alone give 0.32 on my set) and a person rating rendered result grids for 20 to 30 queries, including 'more like #3' follow-ups.
recommendation_for_font_explorer: SKIP for the mood and motion problem; keep it as an optional later add-on for 'more like this'. Why: the published numbers show embeddings help most for similarity, not for mood words (vanilla CLIP 67.7% on similarity but 51.9% on attribute words; FontCLIP 65.3% on words, the same as hand-made features at 65.7%), nothing is published for fast, active, loud, futuristic or techno, and measured traits already give held-out AUCs of 0.88 to 0.96 on those words with a 200-line Node script. Vision labels cover the same 'overall look' signal for about $2-4 once, without Python. Where it would add something the other two do not: example-based neighbours for the shortlist and '#3' follow-ups, and tag transfer for untagged rows. Smallest first step if you want to try: reuse tfrere/fontmap's render and embedding steps on about 300 families (all 339 non-Google rows would be the interesting test), compute the 8-nearest-neighbour same-sub-style share and the tag-transfer AUC, and compare with the 0.32 and 0.88-0.96 baselines before building any search code.
